title: FROZEN Capability Universe and Fixed Probe Set — Primary Evaluation 1 (Semantic Compression)
status: FROZEN (pre-measurement). No probe may be added, removed, reworded, or re-pointed after any measurement is taken, and no capability may ever be deleted because a language (including Quidra) lacks it. Before measurement, a defect found by pre_measurement_validation or by adversarial audit IS corrected under amendment_procedure: the correction is numbered and dated in methodology/CORRECTIONS.md with the superseded text preserved verbatim, and any affected measurement is re-taken. Only changes made after results are observed, or made to improve any language's position, are prohibited (spec 10.4, 32).

provenance_and_fairness_statement.derivation: Corrected 2026-09-17 (remediation R-4); the superseded claim is preserved in remediation_changelog. The 20 capability families are taken verbatim from spec section 6.1.2 and the semantic-fact inventory verbatim from spec section 6.1.3; neither was chosen here. The SUBDIVISION of each family into probes was, however, authored with knowledge of the subject language, and the earlier claim that no Quidra documentation or example was consulted is withdrawn as untrue: probes F04.P1, F04.P2, F05.P2 and F15.P1 as originally written reproduced the shapes, identifiers and constants of Quidra's own README examples for its design laws 1, 2 and 3. Those four probes have had their identifiers and constants rewritten away from the README's, and each affected family has been paired with a counterpart probe chosen to exercise the capability the subject language's design excludes, so the family is scored in both directions. The pairings are: family 4 — F04.P1/F04.P2 (writable alias, non-copying view) paired with F04.P3 (heap object identity); family 5 — F05.P2 (explicit writable-alias passing) paired with F05.P3 (function/closure value passed as an argument); family 14 — F14.P1/F14.P2 (closed alternative set, exhaustive dispatch) paired with F14.P3 (new alternative introduced from a separate unit); family 15 — F15.P1/F15.P2 (compile-time parametric polymorphism) paired with F15.P3 (runtime dispatch through an abstract element type). Each counterpart is a capability that six or more of the ten comparison languages provide as a first-class standard feature, and each is scored by the same rubric text and tie-break question as every other probe.
provenance_and_fairness_statement.quidra_is_the_subject_not_the_designer: Quidra is the language under evaluation, not the source of the measuring instrument. The benchmark's purpose is NOT to make Quidra score well.
provenance_and_fairness_statement.capabilities_quidra_may_lack_are_retaine: Families 2 (uninitialized state), 4 (writable aliasing AND heap object identity), 5 (explicit writable-alias passing AND function/closure values), 8 (explicit overflow/div-zero behavior), 14 (closed sum types AND open extension from a separate unit), 15 (declaration-site-constrained generics AND runtime dispatch through an abstract element type), 17 (deterministic destruction), 19 (concurrency), and 20 (FFI, both directions) are retained in full regardless of whether any particular language supports them. A language that supports them scores higher on Capability Coverage; a language that does not is lowered, per spec 26. This applies to Quidra exactly as to the other nine.
provenance_and_fairness_statement.languages_may_beat_quidra: Nothing in this probe set is constructed so that any one language must win. Probes reward explicit, locally determinate expression of the named semantics whichever language provides it, and penalize hidden behavior whichever language has it.
provenance_and_fairness_statement.no_post_hoc_redesign: Per spec 6.1.7 and 32, this probe set must not be redesigned in response to observed rankings. No ranking has been observed (see no_results_observed_at_remediation). Corrections made before any measurement follow amendment_procedure and are logged in CORRECTIONS.md; corrections proposed after a score exists are recorded as errata in the results and never applied here.

toolchain_binding.safety_mode_clause: Where a language exposes more than one arithmetic/bounds safety mode, the frozen Semantic Compression recipe selects the optimized CHECKED mode, because that is the only mode the evaluated Quidra build provides; the selection is a controlled variable and is recorded per language. Applied: Rust `-O -C debug-assertions=on` (optimized, overflow checks on) rather than `-O` alone, which silently turns debug assertions off; Zig `-OReleaseSafe` (optimized, signed-overflow and bounds checks on) rather than `-OReleaseFast`, which makes both undefined behavior; Swift `-O` (optimized, traps retained) and Quidra's single optimized-and-checked mode are already in this posture. C++ has no checked mode and is recorded as such — that is a language fact and is scored by metrics B and D, not by the recipe. Selecting the checked mode is NOT a P-b deviation for any language; it IS the frozen recipe. Rationale: probes F08.P1, F08.P2 and F11.P1 ask what happens at an overflow or an out-of-range index, and a recipe that answers that question differently for different languages would measure the recipe rather than the language. The same clause would be written if the subject language were Zig, Rust or Python.
toolchain_binding.typescript_strict_clause: `--strict` (with `--target es2022 --module nodenext`) is part of the frozen TypeScript recipe, not a P-b deviation, because non-strict mode is not a production-reasonable configuration under authoring rule R2 or spec 7, and because non-strict mode erases the type-level distinction that probes F12.P1 and F12.P2 exist to measure (`let o: number | undefined = undefined; let n: number = o;` compiles clean without it). Under the previous recipe TypeScript was penalised either way: measured non-strict it lost the optionality it has, and measured strict it was forced to PARTIAL under P-b. Neither is a language fact.

semantic_fact_kinds._note: Verbatim taxonomy from spec 6.1.3. These 13 ids are the ONLY fact kinds usable anywhere in Primary Evaluation 1, for every language, in every probe.
semantic_fact_kinds.value_vs_storage: Whether the construct denotes a value or a named/addressable storage location.
semantic_fact_kinds.mutability: Whether the denoted entity (and, separately, what it refers to) can be changed after the construct.
semantic_fact_kinds.aliasing_writable_aliasing: Whether two names/expressions can denote the same storage, and whether writes are possible through more than one of them.
semantic_fact_kinds.initialization_state: Whether storage holds a defined value at this point, and if so which.
semantic_fact_kinds.type_and_representation: The static/dynamic type and the concrete machine or runtime representation (width, signedness, boxing, layout, reference-vs-inline).
semantic_fact_kinds.conversion_behavior: Whether a representation/type change occurs here and exactly what it does at the boundaries (truncate, widen, round, trap, saturate, error, reject).
semantic_fact_kinds.possible_failure: Whether this construct can fail, and how the failure is surfaced.
semantic_fact_kinds.alternative_value_cases: Which distinct alternative shapes a value may take here, and whether the set is closed and exhaustively handled.
semantic_fact_kinds.overflow_exceptional_numeric: Behavior at numeric limits and on exceptional numeric operands (overflow, division by zero, NaN, negative modulo, shift overflow).
semantic_fact_kinds.allocation_copy_move_borrow_destroy: Whether memory is allocated, whether data is copied, moved, borrowed, or destroyed at this construct.
semantic_fact_kinds.externally_visible_side_effects: Effects observable outside the fragment (I/O, global/shared state change, OS interaction).
semantic_fact_kinds.control_flow_effect: Whether control may leave, branch, suspend, resume, or not return at this construct.
semantic_fact_kinds.lifetime_resource_effect: When the denoted resource's lifetime ends and when its cleanup runs.

authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments._purpose: These rules make 10 implementers produce genuinely equivalent fragments. They are frozen and identical for all 10 languages.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R1_equivalence: Each fragment must implement the canonical_task's OBSERVABLE behavior exactly. Two fragments in two languages are equivalent iff, given the same stated inputs, they produce the same stated outputs/effects and expose the same stated semantic commitments. A fragment that silently drops a stated sub-requirement is not equivalent and is scored PARTIAL or NONE, not FULL.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R2_idiomatic: Write the fragment the way a competent, current, professional user of that language would write it for production code, using that language's normal conventions. Do not hand-obfuscate, do not golf, do not pad, do not add decorative annotations that a normal author would omit, and do not omit annotations a normal author would include. Where R2 leaves more than one form acceptable, R10 — not the author's judgement of idiom — selects which one is measured.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R3_minimality: The fragment contains exactly what the canonical_task requires and nothing else: no logging, no comments, no assertions, no defensive checks, no unused declarations, no main/entry wrapper unless the canonical_task names one.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R4_fixed_identifiers: Use exactly the identifier names given in the canonical_task. Where a language's conventions require a different case style (e.g. snake_case vs camelCase), apply that language's normal convention to the same word; do not rename the concept.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R5_measured_fragment_boundary: Each probe declares measured_fragment. Only the text inside that boundary is counted for Semantic Density (tokens and facts), Determinacy, Locality, and Hidden Cost. Supporting context that the probe declares as 'given' or 'declared elsewhere' is NOT counted as tokens but IS counted as a non-local lookup for metric C when a fact requires consulting it.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R6_compilability: Every fragment scored FULL or PARTIAL must be embedded in the minimal compilable/runnable program for its language and must actually build and run under the frozen recipe. The wrapper is excluded from the measured_fragment. A fragment that does not build is NONE unless the probe explicitly asks for a statically-rejected case.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R7_no_external_packages: Standard library and language-bundled runtime only. No third-party packages, no package manager fetch, no code generation, no separate toolchain, no hand-written assembly. Compiler/runtime flags beyond the frozen recipe are permitted only under support rubric criterion P-b and force PARTIAL.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R8_one_fragment_per_probe_per_language: Exactly 440 fragments exist in principle (44 probes x 10 languages). Probes scored NONE for a language have no fragment; that language's record for that probe carries the NONE justification instead. Each language's fragment count n_L must be published alongside its all-fragments metric figures (see support_rubric.interaction_with_quality_metrics).
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R9_no_probe_substitution: If a language cannot express a probe, record NONE with a documented reason. Do not substitute an easier task, and do not mark it N/A (see na_policy) — EXCEPT where a probe's own canonical_task explicitly names a substitution (F02.P2, F12.P1, F12.P2, F14.P1, F15.P1, F15.P2, F17.P2). In those cases write the named substitute and score PARTIAL under P-a; the substitute is never FULL. This exception exists so the fragment can still be measured by metrics A-D, not so a language can avoid the coverage cost of the missing mechanism.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R10_deterministic_form_selection: Where more than one form satisfies R1-R3, the fragment is the form with the FEWEST TOKENS under the frozen tokenizer of methodology 02. Ties are broken by the form that appears first in the language's official reference or standard-library documentation for that operation. Every alternative form considered must be recorded in the probe's evidence record together with its token count and the documentation citation, so a reviewer can verify the selection mechanically. A canonical_task's OWN explicit preference order (F08.P1, F08.P2, F10.P1) overrides R10; R10 then selects only among the forms that preference order leaves equally acceptable. R10 exists because phrases such as 'the normal choice' and 'the way a normal author would write it' were the dominant undefined judgement in this document and every one of metrics A, B, C and D is computed from the text they select.

probes.title: Immutable local binding of an integer
probes.intent: Measure how the language introduces a named, non-reassignable local binding and how much of its value/storage, mutability, type and representation is recoverable from the declaration alone.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body, (1) introduce a local name `n` bound to the integer value 7, using the form the language provides for a binding that will never be reassigned; (2) as the last statement of the fragment, produce `n` as the fragment's result (return it from the enclosing function, whose declared result is the same integer type). Do not annotate the type unless the language requires it or a normal author would write it. The measured fragment is statements (1) and (2).
probes.measured_fragment: The declaration of `n` and the statement producing `n`. The enclosing function header and closing brace are excluded.

probes.title: Module-level mutable storage plus an immutable named constant
probes.intent: Measure how the language distinguishes a long-lived mutable storage location from a fixed named constant, and how much of lifetime, mutability, visibility and representation a reader recovers from the two declarations alone.
probes.canonical_task: At the outermost declaration scope of a single compilation unit (module / file / namespace / class-static, whichever is that language's normal home for such declarations), declare exactly two things: (1) a named storage location `counter`, of a signed integer type capable of representing at least the full 64-bit signed range, initialized to 0, and intended to be reassigned later by ordinary code in the same unit; (2) a named constant `LIMIT` whose value is 100, of the same integer type, which can never be reassigned and which the language treats as a constant rather than as a mutable variable holding a constant value (use a compile-time/immutable constant form if the language has one). The measured fragment is exactly these two declarations. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can tell which one is mutable.
probes.measured_fragment: The two declarations only.

probes.title: Declaration without initializer, definitely assigned on all paths
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can express 'declared but not yet initialized' at all, and how determinately a reader can tell, at the declaration and at the later read, whether the storage holds a defined value.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) declare a local `v` of a signed 32-bit integer type WITHOUT giving it an initial value at the point of declaration (if the language forbids this, that is the finding — see rubric); (2) write a two-way branch on an already-declared boolean `cond` that assigns `v = 5` in the true arm and `v = 9` in the false arm; (3) read `v` after the branch and return it. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). Do not pre-initialize `v` to a placeholder value; if the language requires a placeholder, that requirement is itself the observation.
probes.measured_fragment: The declaration, the two-way branch with both assignments, and the final read/return.

probes.title: Explicitly uninitialized fixed-size buffer
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can express genuinely uninitialized bulk storage (as opposed to zero/default-filled storage), and whether the fragment tells the reader which of the two it got.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) obtain storage for exactly 16 elements of an unsigned 8-bit integer element type whose contents are NOT specified to be zero or any other value — i.e. request uninitialized storage using the language's documented mechanism for doing so; (2) write the value 1 into element 0; (3) read element 0 and return it. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no documented way to obtain uninitialized storage and always zero-or-default-initializes, the fragment must instead obtain the default-initialized 16-element buffer and is scored PARTIAL under P-a (R9 substitution exception) — the substituted fragment is still written and measured.
probes.measured_fragment: The buffer acquisition, the single write, and the single read/return.

probes.title: In-place increment of a scalar variable
probes.intent: Measure the minimal surface form of scalar mutation and how much of mutability, target identity, overflow behavior and side-effect scope is recoverable from that single form.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared, already-initialized mutable local `x` of a signed 32-bit integer type, write exactly one statement or expression that: (1) increases the value held by `x` by 1; (2) does so IN PLACE, so that a subsequent read of the name `x` observes the increased value and `x` is not rebound to different storage; (3) is written in the form R10 selects from the in-place update forms the language provides (compound assignment, increment operator, or plain assignment). The measured fragment is that single statement/expression. The declaration of `x` is given context, not part of the fragment.
probes.measured_fragment: The single update statement/expression.

probes.title: In-place element mutation of a growable sequence through a name
probes.intent: Measure whether mutation through an aggregate binding is locally evident, and whether the reader can tell that the change is observable through the original name rather than through a copy.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `xs` bound to a growable, ordered, integer-element sequence (the language's normal dynamic list/vector/array-list type) already holding at least 3 elements, write exactly one statement that: (1) sets the element at index 1 of `xs` to the value 42; (2) does so in place, so that a subsequent read of `xs` element 1 through the name `xs` observes 42; (3) does not rebuild, reassign, or replace `xs`. The measured fragment is that single statement.
probes.measured_fragment: The single element-assignment statement.

probes.family: 4. aliasing, references, borrowing, addressing, and dereferencing where applicable
probes.title: Writable alias to an existing scalar local
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can create a second name that writes the SAME scalar storage as an existing local, and how explicitly the surface form announces the writable alias and its dereference.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) declare a mutable local `slot` of a signed 32-bit integer type initialized to 4; (2) introduce a second name `port` that denotes the SAME storage as `slot` and through which `slot` can be written (a writable alias / mutable reference / pointer / inout binding — whatever the language provides); (3) write the value 9 through `port`; (4) read `slot` (not `port`) and return it, so the observable result is 9. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). If the language has no documented way for two names in the same scope to denote the same scalar storage with write access, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason.
probes.measured_fragment: All four statements.

probes.family: 4. aliasing, references, borrowing, addressing, and dereferencing where applicable
probes.title: Non-copying read-only view onto an existing sequence
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can express a borrow/view that does not copy the elements, and whether the surface form tells the reader that (a) no copy occurred and (b) writes through the view are or are not possible.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body, given an already-declared local `xs` holding a growable integer sequence with at least 3 elements: (1) introduce a name `window` that denotes a read-only view/reference over `xs`'s existing elements WITHOUT copying those elements; (2) read element 0 through `window` and return it. The measured fragment is (1)+(2). OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine, without running the program, both whether the elements were copied and whether a write through `window` would be accepted. If the language offers no non-copying read-only view, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason.
probes.measured_fragment: The view introduction and the read/return.

probes.family: 4. aliasing, references, borrowing, addressing, and dereferencing where applicable
probes.title: Two independently obtained handles observed to denote the same heap object
probes.intent: Counterpart to F04.P1 and F04.P2. Those two reward a language that gives explicit storage aliases their own surface syntax. This one measures the opposite capability in the same family: whether the language can produce two separately obtained names for ONE heap-allocated object and observe, with a standard operation, that they denote the same object rather than two equal values. Reference identity is the aliasing form used by the majority of the ten languages and is not scored anywhere else in the universe.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) allocate ONE object of a user-defined or standard mutable reference type holding a single signed 32-bit integer field `id` set to 5, bound to a local `first`; (2) obtain a second name `second` for that same object by routing `first` through an identity-preserving standard operation — for example storing it in a one-element container and reading it back out — so that `second` is not written as a direct rebinding of `first`; (3) bind a local `same` to the boolean result of testing whether `first` and `second` denote the SAME object, using the language's standard object-identity / reference-equality operation and NOT a field-by-field or value equality; the value must be true; (4) produce `same` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). If the language has no standard operation that distinguishes 'the same object' from 'an equal value' for heap-allocated objects, no fragment is written; record NONE with the citation of the rule or documentation that makes it unavailable.
probes.measured_fragment: The allocation and binding of `first`, the derivation of `second`, the identity test, and the production of `same`.

probes.title: REQUIRED spec-6.1.4.B probe — ordinary bare call site f(x)
probes.intent: Spec 6.1.4.B mandates this probe. Measure how many materially distinct aliasing/mutation outcomes for the caller's argument remain possible from the ORDINARY call-site expression alone, before consulting the callee's signature or body.
probes.canonical_task: Given, as context declared ELSEWHERE in the same compilation unit and NOT part of the measured fragment, an ordinary one-parameter function `f` whose single parameter has the language's normal growable-integer-sequence type and whose declaration uses the plainest parameter form a normal author would write. Inside a function body write exactly: (1) a local `x` bound to a growable integer sequence containing the elements 1, 2, 3; (2) a call of `f` on `x` written with the language's plainest ordinary call-site syntax — literally the form an author writes when they merely want to pass `x` to `f`, with NO extra sigil, address-of, borrow marker, copy, clone, wrapper, annotation, or modifier at the argument position; (3) a read of element 0 of `x` after the call, returned as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). SCORING NOTE, binding for metric B: the determinacy count for this probe is the number of materially distinct outcomes for `x` and for the elements `x` denotes — including at minimum {callee cannot observe caller's object at all; callee may read but not write it; callee may write elements observable through `x`; callee may replace/resize the sequence observable through `x`; callee may retain the alias beyond the call; a copy was made so no caller-visible change is possible} — that remain compatible with the call-site expression in (2) ALONE, without consulting `f`'s declaration, signature, documentation, or body.
probes.measured_fragment: The local binding of `x`, the bare call expression, and the post-call read/return. `f`'s own declaration is explicitly excluded from the token count and is counted as a non-local lookup for metric C.

probes.title: REQUIRED spec-6.1.4.B counterpart — explicit reference / borrow / address / inout / dereference form
probes.intent: Spec 6.1.4.B mandates that the explicit writable-alias passing forms be tested SEPARATELY from the bare call site. Measure how determinately the language's dedicated forms announce, at the call site and/or the parameter, that the callee receives writable access to the caller's storage.
probes.canonical_task: Express all of: (1) a one-parameter function `put` that takes writable access to a caller-owned signed 32-bit integer variable and, in its body, sets that variable to 12 (the body is exactly that one assignment); (2) inside a caller function, a mutable local `cell` of the same integer type initialized to 3; (3) a call of `put` on `cell` using whatever explicit reference / borrow / address-of / inout / pointer / dereference form the language REQUIRES or CONVENTIONALLY USES for this purpose, at the call site and/or in `put`'s parameter declaration; (4) a read of `cell` after the call, returned as the fragment's result, whose value must be 12. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4), i.e. for this probe `put`'s declaration and body ARE inside the boundary, because the explicit form may live there. If the language provides no documented way for a callee to write a caller's scalar local variable, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason (wrapping the integer in a mutable container/object is NOT an acceptable substitute for FULL — see rubric criterion P-a).
probes.measured_fragment: `put`'s full declaration and body, the caller's local, the call, and the post-call read/return.

probes.title: Constructing a function value that captures an enclosing local, and passing it as an argument
probes.intent: Family 5 is 'function calls and argument-passing semantics'. F05.P1 and F05.P2 both spend their points on how the ARGUMENT's storage is passed. This probe measures the case where the argument IS a function: whether the language can build a function/closure value inside the measured fragment, capture an enclosing local in it, bind it to a name, and pass that name at an argument position. It is scored nowhere else in the universe, and every probe that previously touched the construct routed around it.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body, given an already-declared local `xs` bound to a growable sequence of signed 32-bit integers holding 1, 2, 3, and an already-declared local `k` of the same integer type holding 0: (1) declare, INSIDE the measured fragment, a unary function value `neg` taking one signed 32-bit integer parameter `a` and returning `k - a` (the negation of `a` displaced by `k`), where `k` is CAPTURED from the enclosing scope rather than received as a parameter; (2) bind a local `ys` to the result of applying `neg` to every element of `xs`, passing `neg` BY NAME at the argument position of the language's standard higher-order sequence-transformation operation (map / select / transform / the standard operation that applies a supplied function to each element); where the standard library provides no such operation, apply `neg` to each element with the language's ordinary iteration construct, still referring to `neg` by name at the application site and never inlining its body there; (3) produce element 0 of `ys` as the fragment's result, whose value must be -1. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language cannot construct a function or closure value at all, or cannot refer to one in value position, no fragment is written; record NONE with the citation of the rule that rejects it.
probes.measured_fragment: The declaration of `neg`, the application binding `ys`, and the production of element 0.

probes.title: Returning an element out of an aggregate — value or shared storage?
probes.intent: Measure whether the reader can tell from the fragment whether a returned result is an independent value or continues to share storage with the aggregate it came from, and whether a copy/move/allocation occurs at the return.
probes.canonical_task: Express all of: (1) a function `mid` with one parameter of the language's normal growable-integer-sequence type, whose body returns the element at index 1 of that parameter; (2) at a call site, a local `xs` bound to such a sequence containing 1, 2, 3; (3) a binding of the call's result to a local `y`, written in that language's normal binding form; (4) return `y`. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine, from the fragment, whether `y` is independent of `xs` and whether the return performed a copy, a move, or shared a reference.
probes.measured_fragment: The full function declaration and body, the call site binding, and the final return.

probes.title: Two results from one call
probes.intent: Measure how the language returns more than one result at once and how much of the result types, independence and destructuring is recoverable at the call site.
probes.canonical_task: Express all of: (1) a function `divmod2` taking two signed 32-bit integer parameters `a` and `b` and producing BOTH the integer quotient a/b and the integer remainder a%b from a single call, using the language's normal multiple-result mechanism (tuple, multiple return values, a small record/struct/data class, or out-parameters — whichever is that language's normal choice; no third-party package); (2) a call site that binds the two results to two separate local names `q` and `r` in one binding construct if the language has one; (3) return q + r. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3).
probes.measured_fragment: The full function declaration and body, the binding call site, and the final return.

probes.title: Fused multiply-add expression on fixed-width signed integers
probes.intent: Measure how much of operand type, result type, precedence, evaluation and numeric behavior a reader recovers from a plain arithmetic expression.
probes.canonical_task: Given three already-declared, already-initialized locals `a`, `b`, `c`, all of the same signed 32-bit integer type, write exactly one statement that: (1) evaluates the expression a * b + c using the language's ordinary multiplication and addition operators and the language's ordinary precedence, with no redundant parentheses; (2) binds the resulting value to a new local `r`. The measured fragment is that single binding statement. The three operand declarations are given context, not part of the fragment.
probes.measured_fragment: The single binding statement.

probes.title: Integer division, remainder, and real division of the same operands
probes.intent: Measure how the language distinguishes truncating/flooring integer division from real division, what the remainder operator does with negative operands, and how much of that is visible at the operator.
probes.canonical_task: Given two already-declared, already-initialized locals `a` and `b` of the same signed 32-bit integer type, where `a` may be negative: write exactly three binding statements, in this order: (1) bind `q` to the integer quotient of `a` and `b` using the language's ordinary integer division operator, or the standard integer-division form R10 selects if the ordinary operator is not integer division; (2) bind `m` to the remainder of `a` and `b` using the language's ordinary remainder/modulo operator; (3) bind `d` to the 64-bit floating-point division of `a` by `b`, performing whatever conversion the language requires to obtain a floating-point result, in the form R10 selects. The measured fragment is those three statements. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine the rounding direction of (1) and the sign of (2) when `a` is negative.
probes.measured_fragment: The three binding statements.

probes.family: 8. integer overflow, division-by-zero, and other numeric edge behavior
probes.title: Adding one at the signed 32-bit maximum, with the overflow outcome determinable at the site
probes.intent: Measure whether the language lets the author SELECT and LOCALLY SIGNAL the overflow discipline (wrap, trap, saturate, error value, promote), and whether the outcome is recoverable from the fragment without knowing compiler flags or build mode.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) declare a local `m` of a signed 32-bit integer type initialized to the maximum representable value of that type, written using the language's standard named maximum if one exists; (2) compute `m + 1` and bind the outcome to a local `o`, using the language's operation whose overflow behavior is determined BY THE OPERATION ITSELF, preferring, in this fixed order, (i) a standard checked operation yielding an optional/error value, with 0 substituted for the exceptional case; (ii) a standard wrapping operation; (iii) a standard saturating operation; (iv) the plain operator — and recording which rung was used and why each higher rung was unavailable; (3) produce `o` (or the substituted fallback integer 0 when rung (i) yields the exceptional case) as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can state, from the fragment alone, exactly what happens at the overflow, without consulting the build recipe. Note that toolchain_binding.safety_mode_clause pins every language that has a choice to its optimized CHECKED mode, so the plain operator's behavior under rung (iv) is the checked-mode behavior for every such language.
probes.measured_fragment: The three statements.

probes.family: 8. integer overflow, division-by-zero, and other numeric edge behavior
probes.title: Integer division where the divisor may be zero
probes.intent: Measure how determinately the zero-divisor outcome is expressed at the division site and whether the language offers a form that turns it into a value rather than an unsignalled trap.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body, given already-declared locals `a` and `b` of the same signed 32-bit integer type where `b` may be 0 at runtime: (1) divide `a` by `b` in a form that makes the zero-divisor outcome determinable at the site, choosing in this fixed order of preference (i) a standard checked-division operation that yields an optional/error value, (ii) an explicit local guard on `b == 0` that selects a fallback integer 0, (iii) the plain division operator if neither (i) nor (ii) is available in that language's standard library — and recording which rung was used and why each higher rung was unavailable; (2) bind the outcome to a local `q`, substituting the fallback integer 0 for the exceptional case; (3) produce `q` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is the whole binding construct plus the final production of `q`. `a` and `b`'s declarations are given context.
probes.measured_fragment: The division/guard construct and the production of `q`.

probes.title: String equality — identity or contents?
probes.intent: Measure whether the fragment tells the reader whether the language's ordinary equality operator on the normal text-string type compares object identity or character contents, and whether user-defined or dynamic equality could be dispatched here.
probes.canonical_task: Given two already-declared locals `s1` and `s2` of the language's ordinary text-string type, both holding runtime-produced strings that may be distinct objects with identical contents, write exactly one statement that: (1) compares `s1` and `s2` for sameness of CONTENTS (not object identity), in the form R10 selects from the forms the language and its standard library provide for that comparison; (2) binds the boolean result to a new local `eq`. The measured fragment is that single statement. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine, from the statement alone, whether contents or identity are compared, and whether user-defined or dynamically dispatched equality could run here.
probes.measured_fragment: The single binding statement.

probes.title: Descending sort of a sequence, plus a scalar ordering comparison
probes.intent: Measure how the language expresses a NON-DEFAULT total order at the sort site — which in most languages requires supplying an ordering as a value — whether the ordering actually used is locally evident, and whether the sort mutates in place or produces a new sequence.
probes.canonical_task: Write exactly two statements: (1) order an already-declared local `xs` (growable integer sequence, at least 3 elements) into DESCENDING order using the language's standard ordering facility, supplying the descending order EXPLICITLY in whatever form that facility takes (comparator function value, key/selector function, ordering or reverse descriptor, or a named reverse-ordering operation); the fragment may not rely on the facility's default order, and R10 selects among the explicit forms the standard library provides; (2) bind a new local `lt` to the boolean value of whether already-declared integer `a` is strictly less than already-declared integer `b`, using the ordinary comparison operator. The measured fragment is those two statements. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine from (1) whether `xs` itself was reordered in place or a new sequence was produced, and whether any allocation occurred.
probes.measured_fragment: The two statements.

probes.title: Narrowing a 64-bit signed integer to 32 bits
probes.intent: Measure how explicitly the language marks a lossy narrowing conversion and how determinately the out-of-range outcome is expressed at the conversion site.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `big` of a signed 64-bit integer type whose runtime value may exceed the 32-bit signed range: (1) produce a value of a signed 32-bit integer type from `big`, preferring, in this fixed order, (i) a standard conversion that reports out-of-range as an optional/error value, with the fallback integer 0 substituted for the out-of-range case; (ii) the language's ordinary explicit narrowing conversion; (iii) an implicit narrowing if the language performs one without written syntax — and recording which rung was used and why each higher rung was unavailable; (2) bind that value to a local `small`; (3) produce `small` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is the conversion binding plus the production of `small`. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can state from the fragment what happens when the value does not fit: truncate, wrap, trap, saturate, yield an error value, or be statically rejected.
probes.measured_fragment: The conversion binding and the production of `small`.

probes.title: Mixed integer and floating-point arithmetic
probes.intent: Measure whether a mixed-type arithmetic expression reveals, at the operator, which operand changed representation and what the result type is — the classic site of implicit conversion.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `i` of a signed 32-bit integer type and an already-declared local `d` of a 64-bit floating-point type, write exactly one statement that: (1) computes the sum of `i` and `d`, including any conversion the language requires to be written explicitly and omitting any the language performs implicitly, in the form R10 selects; (2) binds the result to a new local `sum`. The measured fragment is that single statement. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine the static type of `sum` and which operand's representation changed.
probes.measured_fragment: The single binding statement.

probes.title: Indexed read with a possibly-out-of-range runtime index
probes.intent: Measure how determinately the out-of-range outcome of an ordinary indexing expression is expressed at the index site.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `xs` (growable integer sequence, 3 elements) and an already-declared local `i` of a signed integer type whose runtime value may be outside 0..2: (1) read the element of `xs` at index `i`, using the ordinary indexed-read form R10 selects; (2) bind it to a local `e`; (3) produce `e` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language's standard library ALSO offers a non-trapping indexed read yielding an optional/error value, write that form as a second, separately measured variant labelled `F11.P1.checked`, using the fallback integer 0 for the absent case; the primary measured fragment remains the ordinary form. The `.checked` variant ENTERS NO METRIC and is published as evidence only: it may not be substituted for the primary fragment in any calculation of A, B, C, D or E, it does not change this probe's capability points, and its presence or absence does not change this probe's support level. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can state, from the PRIMARY fragment, the out-of-range behavior: trap/panic, thrown exception, optional/error value, undefined behavior, silent clamp, or silent default value.
probes.measured_fragment: The indexed read binding and the production of `e`. The optional `.checked` variant is measured and reported separately as evidence and enters no metric.

probes.title: Sub-range of a sequence — copy or shared storage?
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can express a sub-range at all, and whether the surface form reveals whether the sub-range copies elements or aliases the original's storage.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `xs` (growable integer sequence holding 10, 20, 30, 40, 50): (1) produce a local `part` denoting exactly the elements at positions 1, 2 and 3 of `xs` (half-open range start=1, end=4), using the sub-range/slice/sub-list form R10 selects from those the language provides; (2) produce the element at position 0 of `part` (value 20) as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is the sub-range binding plus the production of the element. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine from the fragment whether `part` copies the three elements or shares storage with `xs`, and whether a later write through `xs` would be observable through `part`.
probes.measured_fragment: The sub-range binding and the element production.

probes.title: Declared-absent optional integer with a default fallback
probes.intent: Measure whether optionality is expressed in the type, whether the absent case is constructible explicitly, and how the fallback is written.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) declare a local `o` whose type explicitly admits either a signed 32-bit integer or the absence of a value, and initialize it to the ABSENT case using the language's explicit absent-value form; (2) bind a local `n` of the plain signed 32-bit integer type to the contained value of `o` if present and to 0 if absent, using the language's standard default/fallback/coalescing form for optionals (not a hand-written if-statement, if the language provides such a form); (3) produce `n` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no type-level distinction between 'an integer' and 'possibly no integer', the fragment must still be written using whatever absent sentinel the language normally uses, and is scored PARTIAL under P-a (R9 substitution exception).
probes.measured_fragment: The three statements.

probes.title: Optional-preserving transformation by a locally declared function, without an explicit conditional
probes.intent: Measure whether the language provides a standard optional-aware chaining/mapping operation and how locally evident the short-circuit on absence is.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `o` of the possibly-absent-32-bit-integer type from F12.P1: (1) declare, INSIDE the measured fragment, a unary function or function value `h` that takes a signed 32-bit integer and returns that integer plus 1; (2) bind a local `p`, of the same possibly-absent-integer type, to `h` applied to `o`'s contained value when present and to the absent case when `o` is absent — WITHOUT writing an explicit `if`/`switch`/`match` statement, using instead the language's standard optional-aware chaining, mapping, or safe-call operation if it has one, and referring to `h` by name at the application site rather than inlining its body; (3) produce a plain integer result: `p`'s contained value if present, else 0. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no standard optional-aware chaining/mapping/safe-call operation, write the explicit conditional for (2) and score PARTIAL under P-a (R9 substitution exception).
probes.measured_fragment: The declaration of `h`, the binding of `p`, and the final production.

probes.family: 13. errors, failure values, exceptions, and propagation
probes.title: Propagating a standard-library parse failure to the caller
probes.intent: Measure whether a function's declared interface reveals that it can fail, and how visible the propagation point is in the body.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete function `parse_twice` taking one parameter `s` of the language's ordinary text-string type, which: (1) converts `s` to a signed 32-bit integer using the language's STANDARD library string-to-integer conversion, an operation that can fail on malformed input; (2) on failure, propagates that failure to its own caller WITHOUT handling it, using the language's normal propagation mechanism (thrown exception, error-returning propagation operator, explicit early return of the error value, etc.); (3) on success, returns twice the parsed value. The function's declared result type and declared failure behavior must be whatever the language requires or conventionally writes. The measured fragment is the function's complete declaration and body. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine from the declaration alone that calling this function can fail, and from the body where the failure can leave.
probes.measured_fragment: The complete function declaration and body.

probes.family: 13. errors, failure values, exceptions, and propagation
probes.title: Locally handling a failure and recovering with a fallback
probes.intent: Measure how the language expresses local recovery, and whether the fragment reveals the control-flow and cleanup consequences of taking the failure path.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) call the fallible standard-library string-to-integer conversion on an already-declared text-string local `s`; (2) handle failure LOCALLY, binding a local `n` of the plain signed 32-bit integer type to the parsed value on success and to the fallback value 0 on failure, using the language's normal local-handling construct (catch block, match/switch on the result value, if-error form, try-with-default, recover, etc.); (3) produce `n` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine which operations inside the construct are protected, and whether any cleanup or unwinding occurs on the failure path.
probes.measured_fragment: The whole handling construct and the production of `n`.

probes.family: 14. alternatives / sum / variant types and dispatch over alternatives
probes.title: Declaring a closed two-alternative type with per-alternative payloads
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can declare a CLOSED set of alternatives each carrying its own differently-shaped payload, and whether the closedness and the payloads are evident in the declaration.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a declaration of a type named `Shape` with EXACTLY two alternatives and no others — `Circle`, carrying a single 64-bit floating-point field `r`, and `Rect`, carrying two 64-bit floating-point fields `w` and `h` — where the set of alternatives is closed, i.e. the language's own rules prevent code elsewhere from adding a third alternative; (2) a statement constructing a `Circle` with r = 2.0 and binding it to a local `s` whose static type is `Shape` (not `Circle`). The measured fragment is (1)+(2). If the language cannot express a closed alternative set, express the nearest standard construct (e.g. an open class hierarchy, or a tagged record with a discriminant field) and score PARTIAL under P-a (R9 substitution exception). Closedness is scored here; the DUAL capability, extending the alternative set from a separate unit, is scored by F14.P3, and neither result implies the other.
probes.measured_fragment: The type declaration and the construction/binding statement.

probes.family: 14. alternatives / sum / variant types and dispatch over alternatives
probes.title: Exhaustive dispatch over the alternatives
probes.intent: Measure whether the language checks exhaustiveness of alternative handling and whether the dispatch construct reveals the payload binding and the fate of an unhandled alternative.
probes.canonical_task: Given the `Shape` type and the local `s` from F14.P1: (1) dispatch over `s`'s alternatives using the dispatch-over-alternatives construct R10 selects from those the language provides for a closed alternative set (pattern match, switch over cases, sealed-when, virtual method, visitor), writing NO default/else/catch-all arm; (2) compute the area — for `Circle`, 3.141592653589793 * r * r; for `Rect`, w * h — and bind it to a 64-bit floating-point local `area`; (3) produce `area` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is the dispatch construct and the production of `area`. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine that the language guarantees all alternatives are covered and what happens at runtime if one is not.
probes.measured_fragment: The dispatch construct and the production of `area`.

probes.family: 14. alternatives / sum / variant types and dispatch over alternatives
probes.title: Adding a third alternative from a separate unit without editing the original
probes.intent: Exact mirror of F14.P1. F14.P1 and F14.P2 score CLOSEDNESS — that the language's rules prevent code elsewhere from adding an alternative, and that dispatch over the closed set is checked. This probe scores the dual capability, EXTENSIBILITY: whether a new case of an existing abstraction can be introduced from a separate unit and reached through the abstract type, which is the point of open polymorphism in six of the ten languages. Without it, family 14 is scored in one direction only.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) in a unit `shapes`, an abstract operation `area` over shapes returning a 64-bit floating-point value, together with two shapes `Circle` and `Rect` implementing it; (2) from a SEPARATE unit that does not modify `shapes` in any way, a third shape `Tri` implementing `area`; (3) in that separate unit, a call of `area` through a value of the abstract type that holds a `Tri`, with the result produced as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). The second unit is expected here: its augmented build command is frozen in toolchain_binding.multi_unit_recipes, so it is neither a P-b deviation nor a P-e scaffold, and a language forced to PARTIAL or NONE solely by the single-file form of its recipe is an infrastructure defect under spec 10.4 and must be re-run. A language whose own rules prevent an operation set from being extended from outside its declaring unit records NONE with the citation of that rule. Closedness is scored by F14.P1/F14.P2 and extensibility by this probe; a language may score differently on the two and neither result implies the other.
probes.measured_fragment: The `shapes` unit's abstract operation and its two implementations, the separate unit's `Tri` and its implementation, and the dispatching call with its production.

probes.title: One unconstrained generic function used at two element types
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can abstract over an element type once and reuse it at two types, and whether the type relationship between argument and result is recoverable statically from the declaration.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a single function `head` that, for an ARBITRARY element type T, takes a sequence whose elements are of type T and returns the element at index 0, with a declared result type that is T (not a universal/dynamic/erased-to-Object type, if the language can express that relationship); (2) a call of `head` on a sequence of signed 32-bit integers containing 4, 5, 6, bound to a local `a`; (3) a call of `head` on a sequence of text strings containing "p", "q", bound to a local `b`; (4) production of a result combining both, namely the text-string concatenation of the textual rendering of `a` and the value of `b`. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). If the language has no parametric mechanism and only a universal dynamic type, write the nearest standard form and score PARTIAL under P-a (R9 substitution exception).
probes.measured_fragment: The generic function declaration and body, both call sites, and the combining production.

probes.title: Constrained generic function over an orderable element type
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can state, at the generic declaration, the requirement its body relies on, and whether the constraint is checked at the declaration or only at instantiation.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a single function `max_of` that, for an arbitrary element type T CONSTRAINED to be ordered/comparable by the language's own standard ordering abstraction (trait, interface, protocol, type class, concept, bound, or equivalent), takes two arguments of type T and returns the greater of them, using the ordinary comparison form in its body; (2) one call of `max_of` on the signed 32-bit integers 3 and 5, bound to a local `m`, and production of `m` as the fragment's result. The constraint must be written at the declaration if the language supports declaration-site constraints. The measured fragment is (1)+(2). If the language has no way to express the constraint, write the nearest standard form and score PARTIAL under P-a (R9 substitution exception); record explicitly whether misuse is diagnosed at the generic's declaration or only at the call site.
probes.measured_fragment: The constrained generic declaration and body, plus the single call and production.

probes.title: Heterogeneous sequence behind one abstract element type, dispatched at runtime
probes.intent: Counterpart to F15.P1 and F15.P2, which score compile-time parametric polymorphism with a statically recoverable type relationship. This probe scores the runtime form of the same family's capability: whether values of two different concrete types can be held in one sequence through a single abstract element type and a common operation dispatched to the concrete implementation without the concrete type being known statically. It is distinct from F14.P3, which measures introducing a new case from a separate unit; this one measures dispatch through an abstract element type within one unit, and a language may score differently on the two.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) an abstract type or interface `Named` declaring one operation `tag` returning a text string; (2) two distinct concrete types `A` and `B` implementing `Named`, whose `tag` returns "a" and "b" respectively; (3) a single sequence `items` whose DECLARED element type is `Named`, holding one `A` value and one `B` value, such that the concrete type of an element is not recoverable from the sequence's declared element type; (4) a call of `tag` on element 0 of `items`, dispatched at runtime to `A`'s implementation, producing "a" as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). If the language has no type through which values of two different concrete types can be held in one sequence and a common operation dispatched to the concrete implementation at runtime, no fragment is written; record NONE with the citation of the rule that makes it unavailable.
probes.measured_fragment: The abstract type declaration, both concrete implementations, the heterogeneous sequence construction, and the dispatching call with its production.

probes.title: Build a growable integer sequence and sum it by iteration
probes.intent: Measure the cost and clarity of constructing a sequence and traversing it, and whether allocation, element mutability and iteration-time modification rules are evident.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) construct a growable, ordered sequence of signed 32-bit integers containing exactly the elements 1, 2, 3, bound to a local `xs`, using the language's normal literal or builder form for that type; (2) bind a local `total` of the same integer type to the sum of all of `xs`'s elements, computed with the form R10 selects from the forms the language provides for summing a sequence — a standard sum/fold/reduce operation from the standard library where one exists, or an explicit iteration construct where the standard library provides none; every alternative considered, its token count and its documentation citation must be recorded in the probe's evidence record; (3) produce `total` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3).
probes.measured_fragment: The three statements.

probes.title: String-keyed map: iterate entries, and look up a missing key
probes.intent: Measure whether iteration-order guarantees and lookup-miss behavior are evident from the fragment, both classic sources of hidden semantics.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) construct a mapping from text-string keys to signed 32-bit integer values containing exactly one entry, key "a" mapped to 1, bound to a local `mp`, using the language's normal map/dictionary type and normal construction form; (2) bind a local `total` to the sum of all VALUES in `mp`, computed by iterating over its entries with the entry-iteration construct R10 selects; (3) bind a local `miss` of the plain signed 32-bit integer type to the result of looking up the key "b" (which is absent) in `mp`, substituting 0 for the absent case, using the lookup-with-default form R10 selects; (4) produce total + miss as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine whether iteration order is specified, and what an unguarded lookup of an absent key would do.
probes.measured_fragment: The four statements.

probes.family: 17. resource management, ownership, lifetime, destruction, or equivalent cleanup semantics
probes.title: Scoped file handle released on every exit path
probes.intent: Measure how the language guarantees release of an OS resource at scope exit including on the failure path, and whether the release point is evident at the acquisition site.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete function `read_all` with no parameters that: (1) opens the file named "data.txt" for reading using only the standard library (this can fail); (2) reads its entire contents into a text-string local `text`; (3) guarantees that the file handle is released when the enclosing scope ends, INCLUDING when step (2) fails, using the language's normal scoped-cleanup mechanism (destructor/RAII, defer, with-statement, using/try-with-resources, drop at end of scope, finally — whichever is normal in that language); (4) returns the length in bytes of `text`, and propagates or handles the open/read failure in whatever way that language's mechanism requires. The measured fragment is the complete function declaration and body. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine WHERE the release happens and that it happens exactly once on every exit path.
probes.measured_fragment: The complete function declaration and body.

probes.family: 17. resource management, ownership, lifetime, destruction, or equivalent cleanup semantics
probes.title: User-defined type with a deterministic end-of-lifetime cleanup hook
probes.intent: Measure whether a user-defined type can attach a cleanup action that runs deterministically and exactly once at the end of a value's lifetime, and whether the fragment reveals where that point is.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a declaration of a user-defined type `Handle` holding a single signed 32-bit integer field `id`, which performs a cleanup action — incrementing an already-declared module-level counter `released` by 1 — EXACTLY ONCE and DETERMINISTICALLY when a value of the type reaches the end of its lifetime, using the language's own end-of-lifetime hook (destructor, drop, deinit, close-on-scope-exit, dispose pattern, etc.); (2) a block that creates a `Handle` with id = 1 bound to a local, and then ends; (3) after that block, a read of `released` produced as the fragment's result, whose value must be 1. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no deterministic end-of-lifetime hook and only nondeterministic reclamation, express the nearest standard construct (e.g. an explicit close/dispose invoked by a scoped construct) and score PARTIAL under P-a (R9 substitution exception); if the language has no standard scoped construct either, record NONE.
probes.measured_fragment: The type declaration including the cleanup hook, the block, and the final read/production.

probes.title: Importing and using one standard-library console-output facility
probes.intent: Measure whether the fragment reveals which external names enter scope and from where — the dependency-boundary transparency of a single import.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) whatever declaration is required in that language to make the standard console/text-output facility available in this compilation unit (an import, include, use, module reference, or nothing if the facility is available without one); (2) exactly one statement that writes the text "x" followed by a newline to standard output using that facility. The measured fragment is (1)+(2). OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine which names the declaration introduces into scope and which unit provides them.
probes.measured_fragment: The import/include declaration (if any) and the single output statement.

probes.title: A code unit with one exported and one private item, used from outside
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can draw an enforced visibility boundary around a unit and whether that boundary is evident at both the declaration and the external use site.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a single unit of code (module, namespace, package, or file-level unit — the language's normal grouping construct) named `util`, containing exactly two items: an EXPORTED/PUBLIC function `pub_add` taking two signed 32-bit integers and returning their sum plus the result of `secret()`, and a NON-EXPORTED/PRIVATE function `secret` taking no parameters and returning 1, where the language's own rules prevent `secret` from being referenced from outside `util`; (2) from OUTSIDE `util`, a call `util.pub_add(2, 3)` written with whatever qualification that language requires, bound to a local and produced as the fragment's result (value 6). The measured fragment is (1)+(2). A second compilation unit is permitted and expected here where that is the language's normal unit granularity: it is NOT a third-party dependency, and the augmented build command for it is frozen in toolchain_binding.multi_unit_recipes, so it is neither a P-b deviation nor a P-e scaffold. Any language forced to PARTIAL or NONE on this probe solely by the single-file form of its recipe is an infrastructure defect under spec 10.4 and must be re-run under the multi-unit recipe before the result is reported. If the language cannot enforce the private boundary at all, express the nearest standard form and score PARTIAL under P-a.
probes.measured_fragment: The unit declaration with both items, and the external qualified call with its binding and production.

probes.family: 19. concurrency / asynchronous execution where the language supports it
probes.title: Two concurrent computations joined into one result
probes.intent: Measure whether the language has a standard way to run two computations concurrently and deterministically combine their results, and whether the concurrency, the join point and the failure modes are evident.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete fragment that: (1) starts TWO independent units of concurrent or asynchronous execution, the first computing the integer 20 and the second computing the integer 22, using ONLY the language's standard concurrency/async facility as shipped with the frozen toolchain (thread, task, goroutine, coroutine, async function plus its standard runtime, actor, future/promise, structured-concurrency group); (2) waits for BOTH to finish; (3) binds a local `sum` to the sum of their two results (42) and produces it. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3), including whatever launcher/runtime/entry wrapper the language requires to run async code, but excluding a plain non-async `main` wrapper. If the language has NO standard concurrency or asynchronous execution facility at all, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason. A single-threaded cooperative async facility DOES count and must be recorded as such.
probes.measured_fragment: The launch of both units, the join, and the combining production, plus any required async runtime entry construct.

probes.family: 19. concurrency / asynchronous execution where the language supports it
probes.title: Race-free increment of shared state from two concurrent units
probes.intent: Measure whether the language and its standard library let the author express a documented race-free discipline over shared mutable state, and whether that discipline is evident at the mutation site.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete fragment that: (1) establishes a single shared signed 64-bit integer counter initialized to 0; (2) from TWO concurrent or asynchronous units of execution, increments that counter 1000 times each, using ONLY standard-library or language-level synchronization (mutex/lock, atomic operation, channel serialization, actor isolation, or a language-enforced exclusion rule) such that the program is DOCUMENTED BY THE LANGUAGE to be free of data races; (3) waits for both, then produces the counter's final value, which must be exactly 2000. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3) including the synchronization construct and any required async runtime entry construct. If the language has no standard concurrency facility, no fragment is written; record NONE. If the language has concurrency but its semantics make this program race-free WITHOUT any explicit synchronization construct, write the fragment that way ONLY if the language's own documentation states a NORMATIVE GUARANTEE that the specific read-modify-write in (2) is atomic; quote the sentence and cite it in the evidence record. An interpreter-wide lock that serializes bytecodes or instructions WITHOUT making a read-modify-write atomic does NOT satisfy this, and such a language must use an explicit synchronization construct. Verification is objective and MANDATORY: the value 2000 must be observed on 20 consecutive runs, and all 20 outcomes recorded. A run that observes any other value is a failed verification and the fragment is not FULL.
probes.measured_fragment: The shared-state establishment, both concurrent increment loops with their synchronization, the join, and the final production.

probes.title: Calling a C library function across the FFI boundary
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can reach a platform C function using only its own standard mechanism, and whether the fragment reveals the foreignness, the ABI, the argument representation and the safety status of the call.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete fragment that: (1) declares the C standard-library function with the C signature `int abs(int)` as an external/foreign function, using ONLY the language's built-in FFI/interoperability mechanism as shipped with the frozen toolchain — no third-party package, no separate binding generator, no separate build system step beyond the frozen recipe (linking against the platform C library that the frozen recipe already links by default is permitted); (2) calls it once with the argument -3; (3) binds the returned C `int` to a local of the language's corresponding signed 32-bit integer type and produces it as the fragment's result, whose value must be 3. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no built-in FFI mechanism meeting these conditions, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason. OBSERVATION TARGET (not a support requirement; scored by metrics B/D only): whether a reader can determine from the fragment that the call crosses a foreign boundary, what calling convention/ABI is assumed, and whether the call is marked unsafe or unchecked.
probes.measured_fragment: The foreign declaration, the call, and the binding/production.

probes.title: Exporting a function with C ABI and a stable unmangled symbol
probes.intent: Measure the OUTBOUND interoperability direction: whether the language can publish a function callable from C with a stable, unmangled symbol name and the C calling convention, using only its own standard mechanism.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete fragment that declares a function taking two C-`int`-compatible signed 32-bit integers `a` and `b` and returning their sum, which is (1) compiled with the C calling convention / C ABI, and (2) exported under the exact, unmangled external symbol name `add2`, using ONLY the language's built-in mechanism for C-compatible export (extern "C", no_mangle plus extern, export, cdecl attribute, JNI-style external linkage, or equivalent) with no third-party package and no separate code-generation step. The measured fragment is that declaration, its annotations/attributes, and its body. Verification is objective and MANDATORY: build the enclosing unit with the frozen recipe for that language and confirm with the platform symbol lister (`nm`) that a symbol whose name is exactly `add2` (allowing only the platform's uniform leading-underscore convention) is present and defined. The validator itself must first be exercised under pre_measurement_validation V2. For a language that produces NO compiled artifact under its frozen recipe, the N-reason is N-1 and the `nm` field of the evidence record reads 'no compiled artifact under the frozen recipe'; that is a NONE with a justification, NOT an N/A under NA-5. If the language cannot produce such a symbol with only its standard mechanism, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason and with the `nm` evidence or the no-artifact note.
probes.measured_fragment: The exported function's annotations, declaration and body.

spec_6_1_4_B_required_probe_mapping.note: Spec 6.1.4.B requires BOTH: an ordinary call-site expression equivalent to f(x) measured for how many materially distinct aliasing/mutation outcomes remain possible from the call-site syntax ALONE (F05.P1), and a SEPARATE probe of the explicit reference/borrow/address/dereference/writable-alias forms the language provides (F05.P2). Both exist and are scored independently. Remediation R-1 added F05.P3 to the same family: the case in which the ARGUMENT IS A FUNCTION. Family 5 previously spent both its probes on how the argument's storage is passed, so the one argument-passing capability that constructs a callable value was worth 0 points in the whole universe. F05.P3 is scored by the same rubric and the same tie-break question as F05.P1 and F05.P2.
spec_6_1_4_B_required_probe_mapping.glyph_neutrality_rule: Per spec 6.1.4.B, no probe awards or removes points merely because a language spells something with the glyph `&` (or `*`, `ref`, `inout`, `var`, `borrow`, or any other token). Score only the semantic determinacy conveyed by the complete surface form, evaluated identically for all 10 languages.

support_rubric._purpose: Frozen before any measurement (spec 6.1.7 item 4). Applied identically to all 10 languages, probe by probe.
support_rubric._baseline_condition: Support is credited ONLY when the probe can be expressed using documented language features or the language's normal standard runtime/library as shipped with the frozen toolchain, WITHOUT benchmark-specific external packages and WITHOUT code generation. Third-party packages, package-manager fetches, binding generators, separate build systems, hand-written assembly, and toolchains outside the frozen environment all disqualify.

observable_criteria: F-1. Every explicitly numbered sub-requirement in the probe's canonical_task is delivered by the fragment, with none dropped, weakened, or substituted.
F-2. The fragment uses only documented language features and the standard runtime/library bundled with the frozen toolchain version for that language.
F-3. The fragment builds (where the language has a build step) and runs to completion under the frozen recipe for that language, unmodified, producing the stated observable result.
F-4. No third-party package, no package-manager dependency, no code-generation step, and no compiler/runtime flag beyond the frozen recipe is required.

F-5. [DELETED — remediation R-3, 2026-09-17, pre-measurement. The slot is retained so that cross-references to F-6 elsewhere still resolve; no criterion occupies it, and FULL requires F-1 through F-4 and F-6 only. SUPERSEDED TEXT: 'F-5. Every fact kind listed in semantic_facts_expected is DETERMINABLE for that language at the probe (possibly requiring non-local lookup — locality cost is metric C's business, not coverage's).' It was deleted because it counted determinacy inside Capability Coverage as well as inside metrics B and D: it placed no bound on the permitted analysis, so a dynamically typed language could be pushed to PARTIAL on many probes purely for being dynamic, paying once in B/D and again in C, which then enters the harmonic mean. Spec 8 forbids exactly that double counting.]

F-6. The mechanism the fragment uses is not one the language's own OFFICIAL reference or standard-library documentation places under an explicit NORMATIVE prohibition or deprecation for ordinary use. The observable test is a sentence in that documentation containing 'deprecated', 'should not be used', 'do not use', 'must not be used', 'unstable', 'internal', 'no compatibility guarantee', or an equivalent normative form, applying to the mechanism as used here. The exact sentence and its URL MUST be quoted in the evidence record; without the quotation the criterion is satisfied. Documented warnings about the CONSEQUENCES of misuse ('can crash the interpreter', 'no type safety is provided', 'undefined behavior if the pointer is invalid') are not prohibitions and do NOT disqualify. A facility the language documents as first-class but gates behind an `unsafe`/`unchecked`/`@available` keyword — e.g. FFI — is likewise not disqualified, because the keyword is the documented normal way to use it. This replaces the earlier wording 'unsafe, deprecated, discouraged, or reflective', in which 'discouraged' and 'reflective' had no observable test and left Python's `ctypes`, Go's `unsafe`, Java's reflective access paths and C++'s raw-`new` guidance to be argued about on the basis of tone in a manual.

At least one numbered sub-requirement of canonical_task IS delivered, AND at least one of the following observable conditions holds. The condition(s) that applied MUST be recorded by letter in the results record for that (probe, language) pair:

P-a. SUBSTITUTED WEAKER MECHANISM. The observable behavior is achieved only by substituting a weaker but standard mechanism that drops a named sub-requirement — e.g. an open class hierarchy where the task demands a closed alternative set; a mutable container/object wrapper where the task demands writable access to a caller's scalar local; a runtime-checked cast where the task demands a statically expressed type relationship; an unconstrained generic where the task demands a declaration-site constraint; a copying slice where the task demands the reader be able to tell copy from share and the language offers only one.

P-b. FLAG OR MODE OUTSIDE THE FROZEN RECIPE. The behavior requires a compiler/runtime flag, mode, pragma, or preview/experimental switch beyond the frozen recipe, but that switch ships with the frozen toolchain and needs no additional download. NOTE: the frozen recipes pin Rust, Zig, Swift and Quidra to their optimized CHECKED arithmetic/bounds mode and TypeScript to `--strict` (toolchain_binding.safety_mode_clause and typescript_strict_clause). Those settings ARE the frozen recipe, so using them is not a P-b deviation for any language.

P-c. GUARANTEE NOT DOCUMENTED. The standard library provides the shape of the behavior, but the specific GUARANTEE the canonical_task names (deterministic cleanup point, specified iteration order, documented race-freedom, exactly-once execution, non-copying view, closed alternative set) is documented as unspecified, implementation-defined, or best-effort, so the fragment can only approximate it.

P-d. DOCUMENTED ESCAPE HATCH. The only expression available is via a mechanism the language's own documentation marks as unsafe-and-discouraged, deprecated, internal, or reflective (e.g. reflection to reach a private member, a finalizer the language documents as not to be relied upon, an internal/unstable API), while still shipping in the standard distribution.

P-e. EXTRA COMPILATION UNIT OR ENTRY SCAFFOLD. The probe is expressible only by adding a structural scaffold the canonical_task did not ask for and that is required purely by the language's unit granularity (e.g. a second file, a wrapper class, an explicit async runtime block where the task asked for none). NOTE: F18.P2, F14.P3 and F19.P1 explicitly permit their respective scaffolds, and toolchain_binding.multi_unit_recipes freezes the build command for the first two, so P-e does NOT apply to those three probes. A scaffold required purely by the harness rather than by the language is an infrastructure defect under spec 10.4, not a P-e PARTIAL.
